text: Method

We tested 61 models in 84 setups on a reading comprehension and grammar test in native Turkish (not translated): 2,198 questions. A setup is one model with one set of settings. We measured four things: how often each was right, whether its confidence found the answers worth keeping, whether it answered the same way again, and its cost and time.

This page covers the Turkish reading and grammar test. Page images and Hallucination explain their own methods on their pages: Page images under How the benchmark was run and Hallucination under Our method.

groups.title: Worked example: Decider v1.1
text: Perplexity's Decider v1.1 is a decision model; this box follows it through the two-step setup. Its typical latency was 0.233 seconds, at $0.008 per 1,000 questions, against $4.93 for Claude Opus 5.5 alone.

At 99%, it kept 349 answers with 0 wrong and passed 1,849 to the second model (error rate interval 0% to 1.1%), and none of the 12 uncertain questions reached that confidence. Its most confident quarter held 546 right answers of 550 and passed 1,648.

The table replays recorded answers, Decider v1.1 first and each LLM second. With one question per request, no cutoff chosen on half the questions loses more than the 0.5-point limit set before the live tests.

In the live tests, the loss exceeded that limit in four tests, and in 12 of the 14 tests the 95% interval allows a larger loss. One test established a change in accuracy: Decider v1.1, then Sonnet, one question per request, with accuracy 4.73 points lower. Live savings were smaller (see the average-cost caveat).

Across five full runs it changed 0 answers, yet repeated the same wrong answer on 728 of the 728 questions it ever missed. Its ranking score was 0.84. Fastino's GLiDE scored 67.9% against its 66.9%, a difference not established, at about 21 times its cost for the first model's calls.

groups.title: What we found
text: No model led on every measure: accuracy, ranking answers by confidence and confidence that matches the hit rate are separate strengths. Gemma 4 31B, a chat model, scored higher than every decision model except REAX 1.3 and d1-ultra on Reading (90.9%) and Grammar (65.6%), but its confidence matched its hit rate less closely than the best decision models' did.

How a model gives its confidence matters. GPT-6 Luna through OpenAI's Decisions API ranked its answers better than Luna writing its confidence (ranking score 0.82 against 0.69) but got fewer right (63.6% against 68.3%), with a different access method and request size. Among decision models, its calibration gap (2.4 points) was second only to Liquid d1.1's (2.0 points).

Cheaper chat models remain alternatives. GPT-6.1 Sol scored 96.7% at an estimated cost 79% below GPT-6 Astra's (97.6%). Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning scored 98.1%, and the test over all pairs did not establish a difference from Astra.

Erk-14B is Qwen3-14B with extra Turkish training by eCloud. Its calibration gap was 13.5 points against 41.0 for its base, with no accuracy difference detected (45.0% against 45.7%); the training may have changed more than language knowledge.

On Artificial Analysis' Decision Index (English tasks), Jev 1.13 leads with 58, ahead of GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 (54). Our order differs. In both tests, confidence is less reliable on some question types: knowledge and reasoning there, grammar here.

groups.title: The questions
text: The test has 656 Reading and 1,542 Grammar questions in 20 topics, so 70% are Grammar. These results cover this question bank only. We did not test whether they hold in other languages or for other tasks. Reading asks about the meaning of words, sentences and passages; Grammar asks about word endings, word types and sentence structure. We report the two separately.

Topics 1 to 6 are Reading and 7 to 20 Grammar; the Topics page gives each one's results. Each question has five options: guessing averages 20%, and always choosing E, the most common right letter, scores 22.7%. Models can favour some letters whatever the question says.8

An optional exam mix reweights the scores to the Turkish section of the first stage of Turkey's 2026 university entrance exam (TYT): 33 Reading and seven Grammar questions. It is not a score on the exam itself.

TurkishMMLU3 covers more than 10,000 Turkish questions in nine school subjects, and HELM4 sets accuracy beside calibration and efficiency. We study the decision models' own option scores, and using them to decide when another model should answer. We do not know what most models saw in training, so we cannot test whether less familiar tasks cause more mistakes.

groups.title: How we checked the questions and answer key
text: We use version 2 of the question set. Our first copy of the book lost the underline in 196 of 229 questions that point to underlined words, and the numbers attached to words in 186 more; we copied flagged questions again and checked them against the page images. Version 2 changes the text or key of 375 questions and makes 12 more possible to score.

Wrong keys are common in test sets and can change rankings.20 We reviewed 25 disputed cases (confident mistakes, and questions where several strong models disagreed with the key), confirmed 13 keys and removed 12 questions: in six the page image did not settle the answer, and in six the printed key could not be established. We score 2,198 questions; 12 stay marked uncertain, and 493 carry a verified label.

The removal raised most models' accuracy by at most about 0.5 points but mattered more for confident mistakes. Among wrong answers at 99% or more, it removed six of eight for Qwen's yes or no scoring, three of eight for Astra, two of three for Jev 1.13 and two of three for d1. Later runs did not get this targeted review.

For models tested on both versions, accuracy on the repaired questions rose 11 to 30 points, apart from Laya and Laya multilingual, whose accuracy on them did not rise. Removed questions stay out of accuracy and confidence, but their time, tokens and money stay in the totals.

Every setup is scored on the same frozen key, version 2. A fix needs a check against the book's key or a second reviewer, and it rescores every run under a new version; the key changelog lists every change.

groups.title: Models and setups
text: A decision model scores the options we give it, and we used only its pick and its scores. A chat model writes its answer, and some reason first. Luna through the Decisions API counts as a decision model, because the service gives a probability for each option.

A setup is one way of running a model: access, reasoning setting, questions per request and other settings. We tested 84 setups of 61 models. Each name links to its setup's page; the results file keeps each identifier, server and hardware.

groups.title: What we sent and which settings we used
text: Each question went with its lettered options. Chat models were asked, in Turkish, for their answer's letter and, where needed, a confidence score, in a structured reply (JSON); a connector turned the same question into each decision service's format. Most chat setups got 16 questions per request; decision models, Luna through the Decisions API, GLiNER and the Qwen 3.8 setups got one.
Claude Code and Codex runs were closed-book: no web search, no file or command tools, and an empty folder for each request. Earlier trial runs could find the source book online.

A missing answer, a refusal or a letter outside the options counts as wrong. The Decisions API declined 4 questions; GLM 5.3 Flash with reasoning left 128 unanswered when it hit the 65,536-token output limit; DeepSeek's first release with reasoning had the same limit and left 0.
Sampling picks the next token at random by its probability. Temperature sets how strongly it favours likely tokens, top p and top k limit the candidates, and a presence penalty discourages repeats.

groups.title: Does one question per request change the answers?
text: Every decision model got one question per request; the chat models' main runs got 16. So we asked six chat setups all 2,198 questions again, one per request, with the same prompt and settings.
The exact McNemar test uses only the questions one run got right; Holm's correction covers this table. Each run with one question per request is a setup of its own.

An earlier test on 200 questions found no difference: Astra got 197 right with one question per request and 195 or 196 in five runs with 16, and Gemma 137 against 141 in five runs from an earlier server session.

groups.title: Where each confidence score comes from
text: We test each mechanism against the real answers before we trust it. Some services round: Luna through the Decisions API gave 80 distinct scores across 2,194 answered questions, and Celeris 75 across 2,198, none above 97%; our calculations handle tied scores.

groups.title: How Open Jev turns option scores into probabilities
text: Open Jev adds a LoRA adapter, 15.5 million adjustable values (about 0.06% of the base model), and a scoring head to a Qwen model. Each option gets its own prompt, and the head starts from Qwen's preference for "Yes" over "No". Softmax turns the scores into probabilities after dividing them by 2.53, the calibration temperature (see the model card).

Another positive temperature never changes the winning option within a question, but it can reorder confidence across questions. We use the chosen option's ordinary probability, not the rescaled score Jev and Open Jev also offer. Open Jev scored 3.8 points above Qwen's yes or no scoring (p = 0.018 after adjustment), with ranking scores of 0.82 and 0.80.

Its probabilities were too low here. Its highest confidence was 64.98%, yet all 144 answers scored 50% to below 60% were right. On version 1 of the question set, a separate refit of the temperature cut the calibration gap from 22.8 to 3.0 points, while the ranking score moved from 0.8193 to 0.8191; the main results use the released model.

groups.title: How we measure accuracy and confidence
text: Accuracy is the share of scored questions a model got right. The ranking score (AUROC) is how often a randomly chosen right answer has higher confidence than a randomly chosen wrong one, with half credit for ties: 0.50 is chance, 1.00 perfect.

Keeping only the most confident answers is called selective prediction.10 The most confident 20% takes that share of answers with the highest scores and checks how many are right; the 50% and 80% shares work the same way. They describe the kept answers only.

groups.title: Calibration
text: Calibration means that a model's confidence matches how often its answers are right. When a calibrated model says 80%, it is right about 80% of the time. Calibration matters when someone uses the number itself, for example to decide how much to risk on an answer.

Calibration is separate from accuracy: a model can be right often and still give probabilities that are too high or too low. It is also separate from ranking: a model can usually put right answers above wrong ones and still give probabilities of the wrong size.

Calibration asks whether the percentages match the hit rate: of 100 answers scored near 80%, about 80 should be right. The calibration gap (ECE)11 sorts answers into ten confidence groups (0% to below 10%, and so on) and compares each group's average confidence with its share right. It averages these gaps, weighting larger groups more, in points. Zero means a match within the groups, not that every score is right; the chart leaves out groups with fewer than 20 answers.

groups.title: What a refit is
text: A refit changes the confidence scores, not the model's answers. The published ranking score still uses the original scores.

The refit has three steps. Before the conversion, probabilities are clipped to between 0.000001 and 0.999999. First, each confidence p becomes log-odds: ln(p / (1 − p)). Second, the new log-odds are a stretch times the old log-odds, plus a shift. Third, the result becomes a probability again. This is Platt scaling.21 Logistic regression chooses the stretch and the shift. With a positive stretch, the refit keeps the order of the scores it is applied to. With a negative stretch, it flips that order; these models are marked "reversed".

Example: Open-Jev 27B v1.1. Its confidence usually ranked right answers above wrong ones (ranking score 0.82), but its probabilities were too low. Fitted on all questions, its stretch is 4.42 and its shift is 4.30. The table refits each answer, then averages within each band:

This table illustrates a fit on all questions. The published results come from a different calculation. We divide the questions into five parts, keeping questions from the same passage together; each question without a shared passage forms its own group. We fit on four parts and measure on the fifth, and rotate until each part has been measured once. Each part has its own stretch and shift; for Open-Jev the stretch ranges from 4.33 to 4.51. On those held-out questions, Open-Jev's calibration gap falls from 24.5 to 1.0 points.
A refit cannot raise accuracy.

groups.title: Better than a flat guess
text: Better than a flat guess compares two probability errors on those held-out questions (5 folds by passage). The Brier score is the mean squared difference between a probability and the outcome (1 if right, 0 if wrong); lower is better. The flat guess gives every answer the same probability: the model's accuracy on the questions used for fitting. Better than a flat guess = 100 × (1 − Brier after refit ÷ Brier of the flat guess), so 0% means no improvement over the flat guess and below 0% means worse. Every model uses the same five parts, and questions without a score are left out, as in the calibration gap. Hamel Husain's post on decision models also found that calibration did not improve every model.

High accuracy does not by itself force this score to be low. The score measures how much the refitted probabilities reduce Brier error compared with the model's own flat baseline. Example: GPT-6 Astra (low reasoning, 16 questions per request) is right 97.6% of the time and scores 19.0%, while Gemini 3.8 Flash (high reasoning, 16 questions per request) is right 98.1% of the time and scores 6.5%. For models with few wrong answers, the score rests on few cases (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 42 of 2,198), so it can vary more between test sets. A score near 0% means this refit gave no improvement in this test. It does not prove that no method could make the confidence useful.

groups.title: What a score of 99% or more meant
text: At 99% or more, Jev 1.13 got 311 of 312 right (1,886 skipped), d1 273 of 274 (1,924 skipped), Decider v1 21 of 21 (2,177 skipped) and GLiDE 121 of 121 (2,077 skipped); Luna got 365 of 368 through the Decisions API (1,830 skipped) and 693 of 830 writing its confidence (1,368 skipped). Few answers leave wide intervals: the 95% interval for the error rate is 0% to 15.5% for Decider v1 and 0% to 3.1% for GLiDE.

Gemma's letter probability reached 99% on 1,782 answers, 1,450 of them right (about 81%), and fell short of it on 416, which the 99% cutoff skips. DeepSeek's first release with reasoning gave every answer at least 99% (2,198 kept, 0 skipped), and about 92% were right.

groups.title: Can another confidence method make the same answers easier to judge?
text: We scored one fixed set of Qwen 3.8 27B answers, 1,191 right of 2,198, four ways. The ranking score was about 0.51 for written confidence, 0.78 for Qwen's option score, 0.78 for agreement across ten answers and 0.82 for Open Jev, a separately trained model. Written confidence tends to bunch at high values,12 while large models' answer probabilities can match their hit rates well.13
The most common of ten answers scored 54.3%, against 54.2% for written confidence, and only about 85% were right when all ten agreed. Several answers can repeat one mistake.

groups.title: How we tell a score gap from ordinary variation
text: Both models answer the same questions, so we look at the questions only one got right. The exact McNemar test17 asks whether that split is too uneven for equal accuracy. Holm's method adjusts the p values for the number of tests: across 84 selected comparisons, and across all 3,486 pairs for the comparison groups (setups sharing a letter). A result from one set does not carry over to the other.

GPT-6 Astra with medium reasoning scored 0.8 points above GPT-6.1 Sol with low reasoning: of 32 questions only one got right, Astra had 25 and Sol 7. The p value was 0.0021 before adjustment; adjusted, it was 0.16 among the selected comparisons and 0.74 across all pairs, both above 0.05. A p value says how unusual so uneven a split would be at equal accuracy, not the chance that the models are equal.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017 with reasoning scored 0.9 points above GPT-6.1 Terra with low reasoning (adjusted p 1). Not establishing a difference does not show equal accuracy: many language comparisons have too few questions to detect gaps this small.18

groups.title: How we measure uncertainty
text: A result from one question set is an estimate. For the ranking score and the accuracy of kept answers, we draw 1,000 bootstrap samples of the questions with replacement, keeping the 14 questions of seven shared passages together. For small groups, such as answers at 99% or more, a Wilson interval gives an error rate above zero even with no mistakes. A 95% interval comes from a method that covers the true value in about 95% of repeated studies, under its assumptions; it is not a model's confidence.
The live tests report their comparisons without Holm's adjustment. Replays with a cutoff chosen on half the questions average 300 random splits of this one question set, not new question sets.

groups.title: How we chose which answers to keep
text: A cheap model answers first; we keep its answer when its confidence reaches a cutoff, and a stronger model answers the rest. FrugalGPT5 and RouteLLM6 study related routing. We count the first model's cost on every question.

Three rules set the cutoff. The cutoff chosen on half the questions is chosen on one random half (a passage's questions together) and tested on the other, 300 times. The most confident quarter keeps the first model's 25% surest answers, and the fixed 99% rule every answer at 99% or more.

These are replays of recorded answers, with no new calls. The accuracy change compares the combined answers with the second model alone on the same questions. The estimated cost adds both models' calls, without the hardware of a first model we ran ourselves.

groups.title: The average-cost caveat
text: Replay savings give every question passed to the second model the same average cost. In the live tests, the passed questions cost more, so the savings were smaller in eight of nine tests.

In the live tests, the second model answered the passed questions with new calls, on one split of 1,099 questions, and separately answered all of them alone. One split checks the replay; it cannot replace the average over 300.
The second model changes the result: in front of Claude Sonnet 5.5 at high reasoning, GLiDE answered 44.6% of the questions and Gemma 60.9%. The best pair depends on the task and the loss you accept.

Does a decision model's uncertainty (entropy over its option scores) point to the questions a stronger model gets wrong? Weakly: its most uncertain 10% of questions held 11% to 22% of those where Opus, Sonnet or Astra erred, against about 10% by chance.

groups.title: Cost and reasoning
text: We report output tokens, request time and money separately. Services charge by tokens, but token counts of different models do not stand for equal computation.

groups.title: What changes when a model does more reasoning?
text: Reasoning helped grammar much more than reading. In all four pairs we tested, the grammar gain was larger, and every 95% interval of the difference is above 0. Claude Sonnet 5.5, low to high reasoning: +32.7 points on grammar, +2.3 on reading. For DeepSeek and GLM, turning on reasoning also turns on random sampling, so those pairs mix two changes.
Each interval is a paired bootstrap over the scored questions (1,000 resamples, each shared passage's questions kept together). The results file holds them, and reproduce.py recomputes them.

Short output can go with high accuracy: GPT-6 Astra reached 97.6% with about 21 output tokens per question, and GPT-6.1 Sol 96.7% with 25. Other research finds that more computation while answering helps on some problems;7 we show it only for these settings.

groups.title: How we estimate the money cost
text: We multiply each run's recorded tokens by published prices, in US dollars per 1,000 questions asked, including the 12 questions later removed. We use the token counts services reported, without checking invoices; GPT and Claude ran on subscriptions, so we price the same use at API rates. Rates for new, reused and stored input apply separately.

Most rates date from 5 November 2026. Perplexity's price changed between its Decider v1 and v1.1 runs, so their cost difference is not only a model improvement. Gemini 3.8 Flash's price is introductory: it doubles on 1 January 2027, to $1.50 input and $7.50 output per 1M tokens.

Every cost of a model on our own GPUs is an estimate, not measured spending. Where the model's maker lists a price for the same model, the estimate uses it: DeepSeek for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017; Z.ai for GLM-5.3-Flash; Alibaba for Qwen3.8-27B; Fastino for Fastino GLiDE v1.2 and GLiNER2.5 Multi (base); Nace.AI for Drex Max v1; Baseten for Mammoth-1 and Elephant-1; Perplexity for Perplexity Decider 27B v1.2 (local GPU) and Perplexity Decider Flash v1.2; and Cloudflare for Clef and Clef-flash. Perplexity bills 3 input tokens per request more than our servers count, so we add them. Each is estimated at its maker's list price for the same model, from our recorded tokens; our hardware cost is not measured. Where only another public host serves the same weights, we use its list price, with any precision difference in the price's name: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, first release, Gemma 4 31B, Cygnet and Qwen3-14B. Otherwise (REAX 1.3, vLLM-SR d3, vLLM-SR d3-ultra, OneJev 27B, Open-Jev 27B v1.1, Winnow-12B, Erk-14B, Metask-Jev 4B, Liquid d1-2B (open weights), Strands Decider 2B, GLiNER2.5-multi-Decide, Laya and Laya multilingual): Estimated from GPU time: the run's request time x the GPUs its server held x Runpod's on-demand price for an RTX PRO 6000, $2.49 per GPU-hour (read 5 November 2026). A cloud-equivalent estimate, not measured spending. Liquid d1: the run used the free tier (d1:free); its cost is now estimated at Liquid's list price for the same model. Fixed output token charges of some decision services follow pricing rules, not written reasoning.

groups.title: What can these results tell us about understanding?
text: A model may answer a passage question correctly and miss a grammar rule in the same language: performance changes by task, which does not settle whether it understands. These tests measure skills models have, not how fast they learn; Mitchell and Krakauer discuss meanings of understanding,1 and Chollet separates a skill from the ability to learn new ones.2

Reading may draw on patterns shared across languages, and school grammar more on local rules; training, difficulty and format could also explain the gap. Confidence changes too: Jev 1.13's ranking score fell from 0.89 on Reading to 0.72 on Grammar, and Open Jev's from 0.89 to 0.75. An Arize evaluation reports a stronger score for Jev 1.13 on two-label English tasks, a different test.

Stronger evidence would change a question's words but not the relationship the answer depends on, then change that relationship and check the answer follows (CheckList9; McCoy, Pavlick and Linzen14). Teaching an unfamiliar rule would test learning directly. Other work looks inside models15 or tests generalisation across wording and reasoning problems.16

groups.title: What changed when we repeated the same questions?
text: We ran 30 of the 51 one-question-per-request setups five times on all 2,198 questions, and 14 of the 33 setups with 16 per request five times on a fixed 200-question set.

On all questions, Open Jev changed no answers, Decider v1 two answers and SubQ Snap Preview nine answers; Jev 1.13 changed about 14%, d1 10%, Celeris 1 9%, Qwen's yes or no scoring 7% and Qwen with written confidence 44 answers (2%). Decider v1.2 (local) changed no answers, Decider Flash v1.2 (local) no answers, Mercury Decide about 9% and Microsoft-Decision-1 about 13%. On the 200-question set, Astra changed 1 question, Opus 20 questions and Sonnet with high reasoning 31 questions. A model can repeat the same wrong answer, so stability alone proves little.
Gemma's stored repeats, in one server session, changed 0 questions; an unsaved rerun after a restart changed some. The Gemma and DeepSeek repeats have no confidence scores.

groups.title: How we measure latency and throughput
text: Latency is the time from sending one request to receiving its answer, measured from our computer, network and any retries within the request included; a request holds one question or 16. Request time is the time at least one request was in flight, over the requests whose answers were kept, overlaps counted once. It is not a run's elapsed time: it leaves out requests that failed and any pause before a run was resumed. Throughput is answered questions per minute of request time.

MiMo V2.6 Flash (high reasoning) sent 32 requests at a time. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, first release (reasoning on), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017 (reasoning on) and GLM-5.3-Flash (reasoning on) sent eight requests at a time. Gemini 3.8 Flash (high reasoning), Grok 4.7 (high reasoning), Kimi K3.1 Pro (low reasoning), Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B (high reasoning), Inkling Small (high reasoning), GLM-5.3 (low reasoning), Qwen3.8-27B (low reasoning), Kimi K3.1 Pro (reasoning none), Fastino GLiDE, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (high reasoning) and GPT-6 Luna (Decisions API, beta) sent four requests at a time. These choices, along with hardware, network conditions and service limits, affect the measured throughput.

Some early runs recorded the total time but not the time of each request. For those, we take latencies from later runs of the same setup. Perplexity Decider 27B v1, Jev 1.13.0, Liquid d1, Open-Jev 27B v1.1, Qwen3.8-27B (stated confidence, reasoning off), Qwen3.8-27B (yes/no scoring), Laya and Laya multilingual use their four later repeat runs on all 2,198 questions. With 16 questions per request, GPT-6 Astra (low reasoning), Claude Opus 5.5 (low reasoning), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (high reasoning) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (low reasoning) use their five repeat runs on the same 200 questions.
Astra's typical latency is 13.0 seconds for 16 questions (from the 200-question repeats) and 6.14 for one; Gemma's is 3.97 and 0.295 seconds.

groups.title: What these results do not establish
text: The questions are online, so models may have seen them in training (contamination, which few tests measure19); turning off web access cannot undo that. On the 40 Turkish questions of Turkey's June 2026 university entrance exam, public before our October test, 14 models got 24 to 40 right. Of the five we added in October and checked this way, d1-ultra got 34, Jev 1.14 31, Decider v1.2 (local) 31, Decider Flash v1.2 (local) 28 and GLiDE v1.2 (local) 33. These 40 questions are a separate check, not part of the 2,198.

When we replaced the correct option's text with a copy of a wrong one, Astra chose the original letter 31.0% of the time and the copy 28.4% on the 1,660 questions whose options are text, with no established preference (p = 0.19). On the same questions, d1-ultra (12.2% and 11.9%), Jev 1.14 (8.4% and 9.3%), Decider v1.2 (local; 11.3% and 11.2%), Decider Flash v1.2 (local; 8.6% and 7.2%) and GLiDE v1.2 (local; 9.2% and 8.0%) showed no established preference either (p from 0.16 to 1). On the 328 questions whose options are single numerals, Astra, d1-ultra and Decider v1.2 chose the original letter more often, which the numerals' fixed order can explain. That checks one form of recall, not whether the model knew the question.
Reasoning, sampling, request size, precision, server software and server state can change answers. This is one language and one question source; a confidence cutoff for a new task needs its own test.

Method.title: How we tested confidence, cost and accuracy

text: Method

We tested 61 models in 84 setups on a reading comprehension and grammar test in native Turkish (not translated): 2,198 questions. A setup is one model with one set of settings. We measured four things: how often each was right, whether its confidence found the answers worth keeping, whether it answered the same way again, and its cost and time.

This page covers the Turkish reading and grammar test. Page images and Hallucination explain their own methods on their pages: Page images under How the benchmark was run and Hallucination under Our method.

groups.title: At a glance

groups.title: Worked example: Decider v1.1
text: Perplexity's Decider v1.1 is a decision model; this box follows it through the two-step setup. Its typical latency was 0.233 seconds, at $0.008 per 1,000 questions, against $4.93 for Claude Opus 5.5 alone.

At 99%, it kept 349 answers with 0 wrong and passed 1,849 to the second model (error rate interval 0% to 1.1%), and none of the 12 uncertain questions reached that confidence. Its most confident quarter held 546 right answers of 550 and passed 1,648.

The table replays recorded answers, Decider v1.1 first and each LLM second. With one question per request, no cutoff chosen on half the questions loses more than the 0.5-point limit set before the live tests.

In the live tests, the loss exceeded that limit in four tests, and in 12 of the 14 tests the 95% interval allows a larger loss. One test established a change in accuracy: Decider v1.1, then Sonnet, one question per request, with accuracy 4.73 points lower. Live savings were smaller (see the average-cost caveat).

Across five full runs it changed 0 answers, yet repeated the same wrong answer on 728 of the 728 questions it ever missed. Its ranking score was 0.84. Fastino's GLiDE scored 67.9% against its 66.9%, a difference not established, at about 21 times its cost for the first model's calls.

groups.title: What we found
text: No model led on every measure: accuracy, ranking answers by confidence and confidence that matches the hit rate are separate strengths. Gemma 4 31B, a chat model, scored higher than every decision model except REAX 1.3 and d1-ultra on Reading (90.9%) and Grammar (65.6%), but its confidence matched its hit rate less closely than the best decision models' did.

How a model gives its confidence matters. GPT-6 Luna through OpenAI's Decisions API ranked its answers better than Luna writing its confidence (ranking score 0.82 against 0.69) but got fewer right (63.6% against 68.3%), with a different access method and request size. Among decision models, its calibration gap (2.4 points) was second only to Liquid d1.1's (2.0 points).

Cheaper chat models remain alternatives. GPT-6.1 Sol scored 96.7% at an estimated cost 79% below GPT-6 Astra's (97.6%). Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning scored 98.1%, and the test over all pairs did not establish a difference from Astra.

Erk-14B is Qwen3-14B with extra Turkish training by eCloud. Its calibration gap was 13.5 points against 41.0 for its base, with no accuracy difference detected (45.0% against 45.7%); the training may have changed more than language knowledge.

On Artificial Analysis' Decision Index (English tasks), Jev 1.13 leads with 58, ahead of GLiDE and Microsoft-Decision-1 (54). Our order differs. In both tests, confidence is less reliable on some question types: knowledge and reasoning there, grammar here.

groups.title: The questions
text: The test has 656 Reading and 1,542 Grammar questions in 20 topics, so 70% are Grammar. These results cover this question bank only. We did not test whether they hold in other languages or for other tasks. Reading asks about the meaning of words, sentences and passages; Grammar asks about word endings, word types and sentence structure. We report the two separately.

Topics 1 to 6 are Reading and 7 to 20 Grammar; the Topics page gives each one's results. Each question has five options: guessing averages 20%, and always choosing E, the most common right letter, scores 22.7%. Models can favour some letters whatever the question says.8

An optional exam mix reweights the scores to the Turkish section of the first stage of Turkey's 2026 university entrance exam (TYT): 33 Reading and seven Grammar questions. It is not a score on the exam itself.

TurkishMMLU3 covers more than 10,000 Turkish questions in nine school subjects, and HELM4 sets accuracy beside calibration and efficiency. We study the decision models' own option scores, and using them to decide when another model should answer. We do not know what most models saw in training, so we cannot test whether less familiar tasks cause more mistakes.

groups.title: How we checked the questions and answer key
text: We use version 2 of the question set. Our first copy of the book lost the underline in 196 of 229 questions that point to underlined words, and the numbers attached to words in 186 more; we copied flagged questions again and checked them against the page images. Version 2 changes the text or key of 375 questions and makes 12 more possible to score.

Wrong keys are common in test sets and can change rankings.20 We reviewed 25 disputed cases (confident mistakes, and questions where several strong models disagreed with the key), confirmed 13 keys and removed 12 questions: in six the page image did not settle the answer, and in six the printed key could not be established. We score 2,198 questions; 12 stay marked uncertain, and 493 carry a verified label.

The removal raised most models' accuracy by at most about 0.5 points but mattered more for confident mistakes. Among wrong answers at 99% or more, it removed six of eight for Qwen's yes or no scoring, three of eight for Astra, two of three for Jev 1.13 and two of three for d1. Later runs did not get this targeted review.

For models tested on both versions, accuracy on the repaired questions rose 11 to 30 points, apart from Laya and Laya multilingual, whose accuracy on them did not rise. Removed questions stay out of accuracy and confidence, but their time, tokens and money stay in the totals.

Every setup is scored on the same frozen key, version 2. A fix needs a check against the book's key or a second reviewer, and it rescores every run under a new version; the key changelog lists every change.

groups.title: Models and setups
text: A decision model scores the options we give it, and we used only its pick and its scores. A chat model writes its answer, and some reason first. Luna through the Decisions API counts as a decision model, because the service gives a probability for each option.

A setup is one way of running a model: access, reasoning setting, questions per request and other settings. We tested 84 setups of 61 models. Each name links to its setup's page; the results file keeps each identifier, server and hardware.

groups.title: What we sent and which settings we used
text: Each question went with its lettered options. Chat models were asked, in Turkish, for their answer's letter and, where needed, a confidence score, in a structured reply (JSON); a connector turned the same question into each decision service's format. Most chat setups got 16 questions per request; decision models, Luna through the Decisions API, GLiNER and the Qwen 3.8 setups got one.
Claude Code and Codex runs were closed-book: no web search, no file or command tools, and an empty folder for each request. Earlier trial runs could find the source book online.

A missing answer, a refusal or a letter outside the options counts as wrong. The Decisions API declined 4 questions; GLM 5.3 Flash with reasoning left 128 unanswered when it hit the 65,536-token output limit; DeepSeek's first release with reasoning had the same limit and left 0.
Sampling picks the next token at random by its probability. Temperature sets how strongly it favours likely tokens, top p and top k limit the candidates, and a presence penalty discourages repeats.

groups.title: Does one question per request change the answers?
text: Every decision model got one question per request; the chat models' main runs got 16. So we asked six chat setups all 2,198 questions again, one per request, with the same prompt and settings.
The exact McNemar test uses only the questions one run got right; Holm's correction covers this table. Each run with one question per request is a setup of its own.

An earlier test on 200 questions found no difference: Astra got 197 right with one question per request and 195 or 196 in five runs with 16, and Gemma 137 against 141 in five runs from an earlier server session.

groups.title: Where each confidence score comes from
text: We test each mechanism against the real answers before we trust it. Some services round: Luna through the Decisions API gave 80 distinct scores across 2,194 answered questions, and Celeris 75 across 2,198, none above 97%; our calculations handle tied scores.

groups.title: How Open Jev turns option scores into probabilities
text: Open Jev adds a LoRA adapter, 15.5 million adjustable values (about 0.06% of the base model), and a scoring head to a Qwen model. Each option gets its own prompt, and the head starts from Qwen's preference for "Yes" over "No". Softmax turns the scores into probabilities after dividing them by 2.53, the calibration temperature (see the model card).

Another positive temperature never changes the winning option within a question, but it can reorder confidence across questions. We use the chosen option's ordinary probability, not the rescaled score Jev and Open Jev also offer. Open Jev scored 3.8 points above Qwen's yes or no scoring (p = 0.018 after adjustment), with ranking scores of 0.82 and 0.80.

Its probabilities were too low here. Its highest confidence was 64.98%, yet all 144 answers scored 50% to below 60% were right. On version 1 of the question set, a separate refit of the temperature cut the calibration gap from 22.8 to 3.0 points, while the ranking score moved from 0.8193 to 0.8191; the main results use the released model.

groups.title: How we measure accuracy and confidence
text: Accuracy is the share of scored questions a model got right. The ranking score (AUROC) is how often a randomly chosen right answer has higher confidence than a randomly chosen wrong one, with half credit for ties: 0.50 is chance, 1.00 perfect.

Keeping only the most confident answers is called selective prediction.10 The most confident 20% takes that share of answers with the highest scores and checks how many are right; the 50% and 80% shares work the same way. They describe the kept answers only.

groups.title: Calibration
text: Calibration means that a model's confidence matches how often its answers are right. When a calibrated model says 80%, it is right about 80% of the time. Calibration matters when someone uses the number itself, for example to decide how much to risk on an answer.

Calibration is separate from accuracy: a model can be right often and still give probabilities that are too high or too low. It is also separate from ranking: a model can usually put right answers above wrong ones and still give probabilities of the wrong size.

Calibration asks whether the percentages match the hit rate: of 100 answers scored near 80%, about 80 should be right. The calibration gap (ECE)11 sorts answers into ten confidence groups (0% to below 10%, and so on) and compares each group's average confidence with its share right. It averages these gaps, weighting larger groups more, in points. Zero means a match within the groups, not that every score is right; the chart leaves out groups with fewer than 20 answers.

groups.title: What a refit is
text: A refit changes the confidence scores, not the model's answers. The published ranking score still uses the original scores.

The refit has three steps. Before the conversion, probabilities are clipped to between 0.000001 and 0.999999. First, each confidence p becomes log-odds: ln(p / (1 − p)). Second, the new log-odds are a stretch times the old log-odds, plus a shift. Third, the result becomes a probability again. This is Platt scaling.21 Logistic regression chooses the stretch and the shift. With a positive stretch, the refit keeps the order of the scores it is applied to. With a negative stretch, it flips that order; these models are marked "reversed".

Example: Open-Jev 27B v1.1. Its confidence usually ranked right answers above wrong ones (ranking score 0.82), but its probabilities were too low. Fitted on all questions, its stretch is 4.42 and its shift is 4.30. The table refits each answer, then averages within each band:

This table illustrates a fit on all questions. The published results come from a different calculation. We divide the questions into five parts, keeping questions from the same passage together; each question without a shared passage forms its own group. We fit on four parts and measure on the fifth, and rotate until each part has been measured once. Each part has its own stretch and shift; for Open-Jev the stretch ranges from 4.33 to 4.51. On those held-out questions, Open-Jev's calibration gap falls from 24.5 to 1.0 points.
A refit cannot raise accuracy.

groups.title: Better than a flat guess
text: Better than a flat guess compares two probability errors on those held-out questions (5 folds by passage). The Brier score is the mean squared difference between a probability and the outcome (1 if right, 0 if wrong); lower is better. The flat guess gives every answer the same probability: the model's accuracy on the questions used for fitting. Better than a flat guess = 100 × (1 − Brier after refit ÷ Brier of the flat guess), so 0% means no improvement over the flat guess and below 0% means worse. Every model uses the same five parts, and questions without a score are left out, as in the calibration gap. Hamel Husain's post on decision models also found that calibration did not improve every model.

High accuracy does not by itself force this score to be low. The score measures how much the refitted probabilities reduce Brier error compared with the model's own flat baseline. Example: GPT-6 Astra (low reasoning, 16 questions per request) is right 97.6% of the time and scores 19.0%, while Gemini 3.8 Flash (high reasoning, 16 questions per request) is right 98.1% of the time and scores 6.5%. For models with few wrong answers, the score rests on few cases (Gemini 3.8 Flash: 42 of 2,198), so it can vary more between test sets. A score near 0% means this refit gave no improvement in this test. It does not prove that no method could make the confidence useful.

groups.title: What a score of 99% or more meant
text: At 99% or more, Jev 1.13 got 311 of 312 right (1,886 skipped), d1 273 of 274 (1,924 skipped), Decider v1 21 of 21 (2,177 skipped) and GLiDE 121 of 121 (2,077 skipped); Luna got 365 of 368 through the Decisions API (1,830 skipped) and 693 of 830 writing its confidence (1,368 skipped). Few answers leave wide intervals: the 95% interval for the error rate is 0% to 15.5% for Decider v1 and 0% to 3.1% for GLiDE.

Gemma's letter probability reached 99% on 1,782 answers, 1,450 of them right (about 81%), and fell short of it on 416, which the 99% cutoff skips. DeepSeek's first release with reasoning gave every answer at least 99% (2,198 kept, 0 skipped), and about 92% were right.

groups.title: Can another confidence method make the same answers easier to judge?
text: We scored one fixed set of Qwen 3.8 27B answers, 1,191 right of 2,198, four ways. The ranking score was about 0.51 for written confidence, 0.78 for Qwen's option score, 0.78 for agreement across ten answers and 0.82 for Open Jev, a separately trained model. Written confidence tends to bunch at high values,12 while large models' answer probabilities can match their hit rates well.13
The most common of ten answers scored 54.3%, against 54.2% for written confidence, and only about 85% were right when all ten agreed. Several answers can repeat one mistake.

groups.title: How we tell a score gap from ordinary variation
text: Both models answer the same questions, so we look at the questions only one got right. The exact McNemar test17 asks whether that split is too uneven for equal accuracy. Holm's method adjusts the p values for the number of tests: across 84 selected comparisons, and across all 3,486 pairs for the comparison groups (setups sharing a letter). A result from one set does not carry over to the other.

GPT-6 Astra with medium reasoning scored 0.8 points above GPT-6.1 Sol with low reasoning: of 32 questions only one got right, Astra had 25 and Sol 7. The p value was 0.0021 before adjustment; adjusted, it was 0.16 among the selected comparisons and 0.74 across all pairs, both above 0.05. A p value says how unusual so uneven a split would be at equal accuracy, not the chance that the models are equal.

DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017 with reasoning scored 0.9 points above GPT-6.1 Terra with low reasoning (adjusted p 1). Not establishing a difference does not show equal accuracy: many language comparisons have too few questions to detect gaps this small.18

groups.title: How we measure uncertainty
text: A result from one question set is an estimate. For the ranking score and the accuracy of kept answers, we draw 1,000 bootstrap samples of the questions with replacement, keeping the 14 questions of seven shared passages together. For small groups, such as answers at 99% or more, a Wilson interval gives an error rate above zero even with no mistakes. A 95% interval comes from a method that covers the true value in about 95% of repeated studies, under its assumptions; it is not a model's confidence.
The live tests report their comparisons without Holm's adjustment. Replays with a cutoff chosen on half the questions average 300 random splits of this one question set, not new question sets.

groups.title: How we chose which answers to keep
text: A cheap model answers first; we keep its answer when its confidence reaches a cutoff, and a stronger model answers the rest. FrugalGPT5 and RouteLLM6 study related routing. We count the first model's cost on every question.

Three rules set the cutoff. The cutoff chosen on half the questions is chosen on one random half (a passage's questions together) and tested on the other, 300 times. The most confident quarter keeps the first model's 25% surest answers, and the fixed 99% rule every answer at 99% or more.

These are replays of recorded answers, with no new calls. The accuracy change compares the combined answers with the second model alone on the same questions. The estimated cost adds both models' calls, without the hardware of a first model we ran ourselves.

groups.title: The average-cost caveat
text: Replay savings give every question passed to the second model the same average cost. In the live tests, the passed questions cost more, so the savings were smaller in eight of nine tests.

In the live tests, the second model answered the passed questions with new calls, on one split of 1,099 questions, and separately answered all of them alone. One split checks the replay; it cannot replace the average over 300.
The second model changes the result: in front of Claude Sonnet 5.5 at high reasoning, GLiDE answered 44.6% of the questions and Gemma 60.9%. The best pair depends on the task and the loss you accept.

Does a decision model's uncertainty (entropy over its option scores) point to the questions a stronger model gets wrong? Weakly: its most uncertain 10% of questions held 11% to 22% of those where Opus, Sonnet or Astra erred, against about 10% by chance.

groups.title: Cost and reasoning
text: We report output tokens, request time and money separately. Services charge by tokens, but token counts of different models do not stand for equal computation.

groups.title: What changes when a model does more reasoning?
text: Reasoning helped grammar much more than reading. In all four pairs we tested, the grammar gain was larger, and every 95% interval of the difference is above 0. Claude Sonnet 5.5, low to high reasoning: +32.7 points on grammar, +2.3 on reading. For DeepSeek and GLM, turning on reasoning also turns on random sampling, so those pairs mix two changes.
Each interval is a paired bootstrap over the scored questions (1,000 resamples, each shared passage's questions kept together). The results file holds them, and reproduce.py recomputes them.

Short output can go with high accuracy: GPT-6 Astra reached 97.6% with about 21 output tokens per question, and GPT-6.1 Sol 96.7% with 25. Other research finds that more computation while answering helps on some problems;7 we show it only for these settings.

groups.title: How we estimate the money cost
text: We multiply each run's recorded tokens by published prices, in US dollars per 1,000 questions asked, including the 12 questions later removed. We use the token counts services reported, without checking invoices; GPT and Claude ran on subscriptions, so we price the same use at API rates. Rates for new, reused and stored input apply separately.

Most rates date from 5 November 2026. Perplexity's price changed between its Decider v1 and v1.1 runs, so their cost difference is not only a model improvement. Gemini 3.8 Flash's price is introductory: it doubles on 1 January 2027, to $1.50 input and $7.50 output per 1M tokens.

Every cost of a model on our own GPUs is an estimate, not measured spending. Where the model's maker lists a price for the same model, the estimate uses it: DeepSeek for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017; Z.ai for GLM-5.3-Flash; Alibaba for Qwen3.8-27B; Fastino for Fastino GLiDE v1.2 and GLiNER2.5 Multi (base); Nace.AI for Drex Max v1; Baseten for Mammoth-1 and Elephant-1; Perplexity for Perplexity Decider 27B v1.2 (local GPU) and Perplexity Decider Flash v1.2; and Cloudflare for Clef and Clef-flash. Perplexity bills 3 input tokens per request more than our servers count, so we add them. Each is estimated at its maker's list price for the same model, from our recorded tokens; our hardware cost is not measured. Where only another public host serves the same weights, we use its list price, with any precision difference in the price's name: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, first release, Gemma 4 31B, Cygnet and Qwen3-14B. Otherwise (REAX 1.3, vLLM-SR d3, vLLM-SR d3-ultra, OneJev 27B, Open-Jev 27B v1.1, Winnow-12B, Erk-14B, Metask-Jev 4B, Liquid d1-2B (open weights), Strands Decider 2B, GLiNER2.5-multi-Decide, Laya and Laya multilingual): Estimated from GPU time: the run's request time x the GPUs its server held x Runpod's on-demand price for an RTX PRO 6000, $2.49 per GPU-hour (read 5 November 2026). A cloud-equivalent estimate, not measured spending. Liquid d1: the run used the free tier (d1:free); its cost is now estimated at Liquid's list price for the same model. Fixed output token charges of some decision services follow pricing rules, not written reasoning.

groups.title: What can these results tell us about understanding?
text: A model may answer a passage question correctly and miss a grammar rule in the same language: performance changes by task, which does not settle whether it understands. These tests measure skills models have, not how fast they learn; Mitchell and Krakauer discuss meanings of understanding,1 and Chollet separates a skill from the ability to learn new ones.2

Reading may draw on patterns shared across languages, and school grammar more on local rules; training, difficulty and format could also explain the gap. Confidence changes too: Jev 1.13's ranking score fell from 0.89 on Reading to 0.72 on Grammar, and Open Jev's from 0.89 to 0.75. An Arize evaluation reports a stronger score for Jev 1.13 on two-label English tasks, a different test.

Stronger evidence would change a question's words but not the relationship the answer depends on, then change that relationship and check the answer follows (CheckList9; McCoy, Pavlick and Linzen14). Teaching an unfamiliar rule would test learning directly. Other work looks inside models15 or tests generalisation across wording and reasoning problems.16

groups.title: What changed when we repeated the same questions?
text: We ran 30 of the 51 one-question-per-request setups five times on all 2,198 questions, and 14 of the 33 setups with 16 per request five times on a fixed 200-question set.

On all questions, Open Jev changed no answers, Decider v1 two answers and SubQ Snap Preview nine answers; Jev 1.13 changed about 14%, d1 10%, Celeris 1 9%, Qwen's yes or no scoring 7% and Qwen with written confidence 44 answers (2%). Decider v1.2 (local) changed no answers, Decider Flash v1.2 (local) no answers, Mercury Decide about 9% and Microsoft-Decision-1 about 13%. On the 200-question set, Astra changed 1 question, Opus 20 questions and Sonnet with high reasoning 31 questions. A model can repeat the same wrong answer, so stability alone proves little.
Gemma's stored repeats, in one server session, changed 0 questions; an unsaved rerun after a restart changed some. The Gemma and DeepSeek repeats have no confidence scores.

groups.title: How we measure latency and throughput
text: Latency is the time from sending one request to receiving its answer, measured from our computer, network and any retries within the request included; a request holds one question or 16. Request time is the time at least one request was in flight, over the requests whose answers were kept, overlaps counted once. It is not a run's elapsed time: it leaves out requests that failed and any pause before a run was resumed. Throughput is answered questions per minute of request time.

MiMo V2.6 Flash (high reasoning) sent 32 requests at a time. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, first release (reasoning on), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 1017 (reasoning on) and GLM-5.3-Flash (reasoning on) sent eight requests at a time. Gemini 3.8 Flash (high reasoning), Grok 4.7 (high reasoning), Kimi K3.1 Pro (low reasoning), Qwen 3.5 397B-A17B (high reasoning), Inkling Small (high reasoning), GLM-5.3 (low reasoning), Qwen3.8-27B (low reasoning), Kimi K3.1 Pro (reasoning none), Fastino GLiDE, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash (high reasoning) and GPT-6 Luna (Decisions API, beta) sent four requests at a time. These choices, along with hardware, network conditions and service limits, affect the measured throughput.

Some early runs recorded the total time but not the time of each request. For those, we take latencies from later runs of the same setup. Perplexity Decider 27B v1, Jev 1.13.0, Liquid d1, Open-Jev 27B v1.1, Qwen3.8-27B (stated confidence, reasoning off), Qwen3.8-27B (yes/no scoring), Laya and Laya multilingual use their four later repeat runs on all 2,198 questions. With 16 questions per request, GPT-6 Astra (low reasoning), Claude Opus 5.5 (low reasoning), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (high reasoning) and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (low reasoning) use their five repeat runs on the same 200 questions.
Astra's typical latency is 13.0 seconds for 16 questions (from the 200-question repeats) and 6.14 for one; Gemma's is 3.97 and 0.295 seconds.

groups.title: What these results do not establish
text: The questions are online, so models may have seen them in training (contamination, which few tests measure19); turning off web access cannot undo that. On the 40 Turkish questions of Turkey's June 2026 university entrance exam, public before our October test, 14 models got 24 to 40 right. Of the five we added in October and checked this way, d1-ultra got 34, Jev 1.14 31, Decider v1.2 (local) 31, Decider Flash v1.2 (local) 28 and GLiDE v1.2 (local) 33. These 40 questions are a separate check, not part of the 2,198.

groups.title: Backgammon in one page
text: The goal. Two players race their 15 checkers around the board and off it. The first player to bear off all 15 checkers wins.
The board. The board has 24 narrow triangles, called points. Each player moves in the opposite direction. Each player's last six points are their home board.

Moving. A player rolls two dice and moves checkers by those two numbers. One checker can take both numbers, or two checkers can take one each. A roll of doubles (for example 4-4) is played four times. A checker cannot land on a point that holds two or more of the opponent's checkers.

Hitting. A single checker alone on a point is a blot. If the opponent lands on it, the blot is hit: it goes to the middle of the board (the bar). It must come back in through the opponent's home board before any other checker can move. Being hit costs a lot of time in the race.
Bearing off. When all 15 of a player's checkers are in their home board, that player can start taking them off the board.

groups.title: Rules of backgammon, as the prompt states them
text: The rules as every player reads them in the prompt (bg-v2, the current version: Method: The prompt), quoted unchanged.

The board has 24 points in a horseshoe-shaped track, 12 on each side. Each player numbers the points from their own side, 1 to 24, and moves from the 24-point toward the 1-point; the two players move in opposite directions. Each player starts with 15 checkers: two on the 24-point, five on the 13-point (the midpoint), three on the 8-point, and five on the 6-point.
Points 1-6 are your home board and points 7-12 your outer board. The 7-point is the bar point.

Once all 15 of your checkers are in your home board, you may bear them off: a 1 removes a checker from the 1-point, a 2 from the 2-point, and so on. A die higher than your highest occupied point removes a checker from that highest point. For example, with 6-5, no checkers on the 6-point, and two on the 5-point, both checkers come off the 5-point. A checker hit during the bear-off must enter and come home before bearing off continues.
The first player to bear off all 15 checkers wins:

groups.title: Setup
text: The question is which model, at which reasoning setting, makes better decisions in which positions. Two kinds of data answer it: league games and shared positions. A setup is one model with one set of settings: the same model at a lower and a higher reasoning effort is two setups. A setup is named by what its requests sent, checked in the request logs: (low), (medium), (high) = the effort level sent; (off) = reasoning turned off, no reasoning tokens; (on) = thinking switched on where the model offers no effort levels (its chat template's default).

groups.title: Leagues
text: Setups play each other in leagues: each league is a single round robin. League tables compare players inside one league only, and leagues are never merged into one overall score. See Leagues.

groups.title: Shared positions
text: Every setup answers the same fixed positions with the same prompt. These positions, not the league tables, compare setups across leagues, and the main ranking uses them only. Each position is a board, the dice and the side to move.

Counts from the position build log. Sampling rules: every position has 2 to 25 legal plays, so no model needs its plays split into groups; each self-play game gives at most one position per phase; within a game and phase the turn is drawn at random from a fixed seed; duplicates are skipped. If a phase cannot be filled, all distinct positions are used and the shortfall is logged.

groups.title: History
text: The prompt was built one step at a time in the earlier version's leagues; the next section shows each step and what it changed. bg-v2 keeps that format and changes how the models are asked: the plays are shuffled, an invalid answer is not retried, and every setup gets the same rules and question. The earlier version re-asked up to three times and then played the first legal play, which its order favoured.

groups.title: Why it looks like this
text: Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.
The prompt was changed one step at a time, and a league was run after each step. Leagues stopped part-way are kept, with their finished matches only.

Grey rows did not finish. "Best opening play" is the share of first moves of a game that match the computer-rollout table in the prompt. "Error rate" is GNU Backgammon's, over all model decisions of the league (see Error rate); lower is better. Leagues #2, #4, #5, #9 and #10 failed at start or were stopped within minutes; league #3 is left out of the standings below because its format differs.

groups.title: Rules and strategy as text, not a data structure
text: The first leagues sent the position as structured data with a short rules summary. Models opened badly: 28% of first moves matched the known best play. With the rules, strategy principles and the opening table as prose, that rose to 77%. Opening play improved, but the middle game did not: games still ran to the turn limit, because both sides kept hitting and re-entering.

groups.title: A question that names what a good move does
text: The question before the choices states three goals in plain words: build a point in front of the opponent's checkers, reduce your blots, bring checkers home. It deliberately leaves hitting out, because hitting on almost every move was the problem. The turn-limit share fell from 81% to 71% (this league also switched to the self-hosted Decider v1.1); hitting barely changed.

groups.title: Compute the consequences in code, not in the model
text: Backgammon decisions turn on numbers a language model cannot work out reliably from a list of notations: which checkers are left alone, how many of the opponent's 36 rolls hit them, which points are made. Earlier, each option was just its notation, like bar/19 13/11*, and the model had to imagine the resulting position. Now the program computes those numbers for every option and the model compares them. This is the change that ended the endless games: hits fell from about 60% to under 10% of moves and the average game from about 270 turns to about 50.

Opening play got worse at the same time, from about 80% to between 58% and 69% best plays. The metrics after each option compete with the opening table earlier in the prompt, and on the first move several plays look similar on these numbers.

groups.title: Recent moves, for longer plans
text: Each decision is a separate request, so a model cannot see how the position came about. League #13 adds the last 10 moves of the game, both sides. Ten turns add about 200 tokens. More would eat into Open-Jev's 4,096-token limit, which it applies to the whole question repeated for every option.

It made no measurable difference. League #13's error rate was 39.1 (± 2.2), against 38.6 (± 1.2) for #8, #11 and #12 together, and the finishing order barely changed. Ten moves may be too few, or these models may not use them.

groups.title: Error rate
text: Wins and losses depend heavily on the dice. A backgammon engine can instead judge every decision directly. GNU Backgammon 1.08 evaluates every legal play at 2-ply, in cubeless money equity (expected points per game, match score ignored). The loss of a decision is the equity of the best play minus the equity of the play made. A play that ends the game scores its points exactly.

text: The core question: when a model takes a risk, is it the right risk? And when it plays safe, was safe right? The thresholds below (0.001, 0.02, the stake bands 0.02 and 0.08) were fixed on 2026-10-23, before any of these numbers was computed.

groups.title: Ability and caution
text: Results published: ability, caution, aim and the cost-derived SDT reference are on the home page's Risk tab (table and chart).

In plain words: ability is how well a setup tells Risk pays positions from Safety pays positions; caution is how much evidence it needs before it takes a risk. A setup can be able and cautious, able and bold, and so on; the two are read separately. Both use the risk classes and risk calls above, at each margin, for every setup and reference row with decisions.

groups.title: Reference rows
text: Shown, never ranked, never champions. Random plays a random legal play; GNUbg weak is the x86-64 build: its noise is shifted, so it overplays gammons (see The anchor).

Safest is not the same thing in every league. In League 1, Safest is the program that actually played the matches: among the plays that leave the fewest hitting rolls it takes the one with the fewest blots, then the largest pip lead, then the play shown first; it never asks the engine. It played a fewest-hitting-rolls play in 2,058 of its 2,058 scored decisions and the engine's best safe play in 1,395 of them. Its right-safety part of the error rate, 8.45 PR, is the equity lost on its 749 right-safety decisions × 500 ÷ all 2,058 of its scored decisions: a share of its error rate, not the average loss of a right-safety decision, which is 23.22 PR. In League 2 and League 3, Safest (computed) is a computed reference: the engine's best safe play on every scored decision of that league. Its numbers are not directly comparable with League 1's played program.

Random also played League 1 only; in the other leagues it is computed as the expectation over all legal plays, so its counts can have decimals. A cell with no decisions shows its count, 0, and no average.

groups.title: Setup
text: The question is which model, at which reasoning setting, makes better decisions in which positions. Two kinds of data answer it: league games and shared positions. A setup is one model with one set of settings: the same model at a lower and a higher reasoning effort is two setups. A setup is named by what its requests sent, checked in the request logs: (low), (medium), (high) = the effort level sent; (off) = reasoning turned off, no reasoning tokens; (on) = thinking switched on where the model offers no effort levels (its chat template's default).

groups.title: Leagues
text: Setups play each other in leagues: each league is a single round robin. League tables compare players inside one league only, and leagues are never merged into one overall score. See Leagues.

groups.title: Shared positions
text: Every setup answers the same fixed positions with the same prompt. These positions, not the league tables, compare setups across leagues, and the main ranking uses them only. Each position is a board, the dice and the side to move.

Counts from the position build log. Sampling rules: every position has 2 to 25 legal plays, so no model needs its plays split into groups; each self-play game gives at most one position per phase; within a game and phase the turn is drawn at random from a fixed seed; duplicates are skipped. If a phase cannot be filled, all distinct positions are used and the shortfall is logged.

groups.title: The prompt
text: The current version is bg-v2. Every player gets it, and it did not change after the first match. It is the format of the earlier version's league #8. Every decision sends these parts in this order:
There is no move history: in the earlier version, adding the last 10 moves made no measurable difference. The Every decision page shows the exact text each model was sent.

groups.title: History
text: The prompt was built one step at a time in the earlier version's leagues; the next section shows each step and what it changed. bg-v2 keeps that format and changes how the models are asked: the plays are shuffled, an invalid answer is not retried, and every setup gets the same rules and question. groups.title: Why it looks like this
text: Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early.
The prompt was changed one step at a time, and a league was run after each step. Leagues stopped part-way are kept, with their finished matches only.

Grey rows did not finish. "Best opening play" is the share of first moves of a game that match the computer-rollout table in the prompt. "Error rate" is GNU Backgammon's, over all model decisions of the league (see Error rate); lower is better. Leagues #2, #4, #5, #9 and #10 failed at start or were stopped within minutes; league #3 is left out of the standings below because its format differs.

groups.title: Rules and strategy as text, not a data structure
text: The first leagues sent the position as structured data with a short rules summary. Models opened badly: 28% of first moves matched the known best play. With the rules, strategy principles and the opening table as prose, that rose to 77%. Opening play improved, but the middle game did not: games still ran to the turn limit, because both sides kept hitting and re-entering.

groups.title: A question that names what a good move does
text: The question before the choices states three goals in plain words: build a point in front of the opponent's checkers, reduce your blots, bring checkers home. It deliberately leaves hitting out, because hitting on almost every move was the problem. The turn-limit share fell from 81% to 71% (this league also switched to the self-hosted Decider v1.1); hitting barely changed.

groups.title: Compute the consequences in code, not in the model
text: Backgammon decisions turn on numbers a language model cannot work out reliably from a list of notations: which checkers are left alone, how many of the opponent's 36 rolls hit them, which points are made. Earlier, each option was just its notation, like bar/19 13/11*, and the model had to imagine the resulting position. Now the program computes those numbers for every option and the model compares them. This is the change that ended the endless games: hits fell from about 60% to under 10% of moves and the average game from about 270 turns to about 50.

Opening play got worse at the same time, from about 80% to between 58% and 69% best plays. The metrics after each option compete with the opening table earlier in the prompt, and on the first move several plays look similar on these numbers.

groups.title: Recent moves, for longer plans
text: Each decision is a separate request, so a model cannot see how the position came about. League #13 adds the last 10 moves of the game, both sides. Ten turns add about 200 tokens. More would eat into Open-Jev's 4,096-token limit, which it applies to the whole question repeated for every option.

It made no measurable difference. League #13's error rate was 39.1 (± 2.2), against 38.6 (± 1.2) for #8, #11 and #12 together, and the finishing order barely changed. Ten moves may be too few, or these models may not use them.

A real request from league #13, Jev 1.13.0 to move (the rules part is left out):

The numbers after each play are exact. The opponent's hitting rolls are counted by generating its legal plays for each of the 36 rolls and checking whether any of them hits. In the example the model narrowly preferred the play with one blot that every roll hits over the one with two blots that 31 rolls hit.

groups.title: Error rate
text: Wins and losses depend heavily on the dice. A backgammon engine can instead judge every decision directly. GNU Backgammon 1.08 evaluates every legal play at 2-ply, in cubeless money equity (expected points per game, match score ignored). The loss of a decision is the equity of the best play minus the equity of the play made. A play that ends the game scores its points exactly.

groups.title: Human scale (approximate)
text: Error rates are shown next to eXtreme Gammon rating scale's bands for human players:

The comparison is approximate. Human ratings also count doubling-cube decisions; these games have no cube, so the error rate covers checker plays only. The scale also comes from eXtreme Gammon's own evaluation, not GNU Backgammon at 2-ply. Read a band as a rough guide, not as a measured human level.

groups.title: Was it the right risk? Definitions
text: The core question: when a model takes a risk, is it the right risk? And when it plays safe, was safe right? The thresholds below (0.001, 0.02, the stake bands 0.02 and 0.08) were fixed on 2026-10-23, before any of these numbers was computed.

groups.title: Metrics per setup (the Risk tab, in this order)
text: Every share shows its count and denominator. Every metric is computed per league; league comparisons are not paired. Setups met different positions, and risk judgement is not adjusted for how hard they were; paired comparisons wait for the shared positions.

groups.title: Ability and caution
text: Results published: ability, caution, aim and the cost-derived SDT reference are on the home page's Risk tab (table and chart).

In plain words: ability is how well a setup tells Risk pays positions from Safety pays positions; caution is how much evidence it needs before it takes a risk. A setup can be able and cautious, able and bold, and so on; the two are read separately. Both use the risk classes and risk calls above, at each margin, for every setup and reference row with decisions.

groups.title: Reference rows
text: Shown, never ranked, never champions. Random plays a random legal play; GNUbg weak is the x86-64 build: its noise is shifted, so it overplays gammons (see The anchor).

Safest is not the same thing in every league. In League 1, Safest is the program that actually played the matches: among the plays that leave the fewest hitting rolls it takes the one with the fewest blots, then the largest pip lead, then the play shown first; it never asks the engine. It played a fewest-hitting-rolls play in 2,058 of its 2,058 scored decisions and the engine's best safe play in 1,395 of them. Its right-safety part of the error rate, 8.45 PR, is the equity lost on its 749 right-safety decisions × 500 ÷ all 2,058 of its scored decisions: a share of its error rate, not the average loss of a right-safety decision, which is 23.22 PR. In League 2 and League 3, Safest (computed) is a computed reference: the engine's best safe play on every scored decision of that league. Its numbers are not directly comparable with League 1's played program.

Random also played League 1 only; in the other leagues it is computed as the expectation over all legal plays, so its counts can have decimals. A cell with no decisions shows its count, 0, and no average.

groups.title: Charts
text: Risk map: across, the Risk pays decisions without the right risk (missed + wrong risks) as a share of Risk pays decisions; up, needless risks as a share of Safety pays decisions. Risk judgement = 100 − (across + up) / 2, so the corner (0, 0) is risk judgement 100; the faint diagonals mark 50, 60, 70, 80, 90. A point's colour is its share of wrong risks among the Risk pays decisions without the right risk. Error rate by risk-call category: the six parts as a stacked bar. Stake chart: risks found, wrong and missed risks per stake band, and big needless risks. Ability and caution: ability across, caution up, programs and computed reference rows as squares, a short bar at the cost-derived SDT reference where it is valid; under it the limit line: a simple model of the risk call (equal-variance signal detection); setups met different positions. Risk call card: one image per league winner. A downloaded chart PNG carries the site's title and subtitle, the league, the margin, the number of decisions, the results version and the site address, and lists the active filters; it keeps the theme in view. Every table on the site has its own Download PNG: the table as shown (tab, filters, sort, theme) with all its columns and rows, the headings above it and the notes under it, then the same small type, with the rows shown and the decisions behind them.

groups.title: Robustness: the 0.02 margin
text: At 2-ply the engine can misjudge close plays by more than 0.001. Every risk metric is therefore computed a second time with 0.02 in every place where 0.001 appears above. The 0.02 results are on the Risk tab under the main table, and here:

groups.title: Versions and play order
text: Numbers from different benchmark versions or prompt formats are never put in one ranking or chart. Every number carries its version.

Earlier version Plays were listed in the runner's order, which tends to put the best play early. Re-asked with the same plays in a random order on 1,000 positions, Gemini 4 Argon's error rate changed by +1.9 (95% interval −0.2 to 4.2), so a help from the order is possible but not proven. The current version shuffles the plays for every setup.

groups.title: Can a model predict where it will waver?
text: Stage B: five teams
Close choices: does a setup know where it hesitates?
Scope. Gemma 4 31B (on) was started but not completed: two reboots and a GPU fault interrupted it, and it was stopped after 311 of 500 play calls on 2026-10-25. Its partial data is not reported.

Each team answered the same 100 positions 5 times, and once more in a separate call naming the features it expects to differ between the plays it might choose (hitting risk, making a point, the race, the prime). Observed set: the features that differ between any of the 5 chosen plays. Primary score: exact agreement of the predicted set with the observed set. Secondary score, declared secondary: partial overlap of the two sets. Baseline: the team's own predictions shuffled within phase, 1,000 seeded shuffles; p = the share of shuffles scoring at least the observed mean. Stage B asks again and looks at repeated answers; it is separate from stage A (Confidence tab), which reads recorded league decisions.
Not a ranking: each team is compared with its own shuffled baseline, never with another team. Rows are in fixed alphabetical order and the table cannot be sorted.
